I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

I can't rely on other people
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these two items directly contradict each other: being able to talk about the trauma very easily is inconsistent with losing the thread and being unable to finish when trying to explain it. Partial clarity could coexist with fragmented recall, but not with both easy verbal access and marked inability to narrate the event.

vignette:
Ethan is a 32-year-old park ranger who, until six months ago, found a deep sense of peace in the sprawling wilderness he patrolled. That peace was shattered during a conservation exchange program abroad. While driving a supply jeep down a remote dirt road, his vehicle was ambushed. The sudden stop, the shouting in a language he didn't understand, the rough hands pulling him from the cab-these moments are searingly, vividly clear. What followed is a blur of darkness, punctuated by flashes of excruciating pain and long stretches of silent, terrifying waiting. He was held for three days, and the uncertainty of those long delays, never knowing what was coming next, was a unique form of torment. He eventually escaped during a transfer, but the experience followed him home, seeping into the quiet solitude of his life and work.

The memory of what happened refuses to settle into a coherent story. When Ethan tries to explain it, the words catch in his throat, and the narrative thread disintegrates. He is left with a collection of sensory fragments: the dusty smell of the burlap sack forced over his head, the sharp, metallic taste of fear, the exact pattern of the water stains on the ceiling of the room where he was held. This inability to articulate the event has become a source of immense distress; it feels like proof that his mind is broken, feeding a terrifying belief that he is going crazy. These memory fragments often surface without warning, and because they are so disjointed, his body reacts with a jolt of panic before he has even had time to process what he is remembering. To manage this internal chaos, he has learned to push all feeling down, cultivating a flat, empty numbness that keeps the worst of the memories at bay, at least for a while.

His internal world is now governed by a set of harsh, unshakeable beliefs that grew out of the helplessness he felt. He is convinced that his body has been permanently damaged by the ordeal, leaving him fragile and vulnerable. This conviction that he is irrevocably broken seems to pull the memory closer, forcing him to scan the fragmented images of the attack for the exact moment the damage was done. This deep sense of physical vulnerability has transformed his perception of the world into a place of constant, imminent danger. When a meeting with his supervisor is pushed back an hour, he doesn't feel relief; he feels a surge of dread, certain that the delay means something terrible is about to happen. At home, he finds himself checking and re-checking the locks on his doors and windows, sometimes three or four times before he can attempt to rest. The core belief that he cannot rely on other people-forged in the days when no one came for him-has made him intensely wary. Before any interaction, even a simple phone call to the park's main office, he must meticulously rehearse what he is going to say, trying to control for every possible variable in a world he no longer trusts.

This pervasive sense of threat has, in turn, reshaped his life and his mind. The constant, thrumming anxiety makes it impossible to calmly reflect on the past; any attempt to piece together what happened is immediately overwhelmed by a wave of panic, which serves only to further shatter the memory into frightening, disconnected pieces. The feeling of his heart pounding in his chest when a car backfires nearby provides visceral confirmation for his fear that he is losing control, that his reactions are no longer his own. To manage this overwhelming state of alarm, Ethan has begun to avoid anything that reminds him of the initial capture. He has all but stopped driving. As a park ranger, this has been catastrophic. He can no longer patrol the vast outer loops of the park, confining himself to a small, walkable area around the main station, his world shrinking daily.

These strategies, born of desperation, now form a self-reinforcing prison. The more he avoids driving, the more the act of being in a vehicle feels insurmountably dangerous, reinforcing his sense of threat. The emotional numbing he relies on prevents any real processing of the trauma, ensuring the memories remain stuck as raw, potent fragments that can ambush him at any time. This failure to "get over it" deepens his conviction that he is permanently broken and fundamentally different from everyone else. He came to therapy after his supervisor, noticing his abandoned patrol routes, gave him a final warning. Ethan spoke in a low, controlled monotone, the effort of holding himself together evident in his rigid posture. His greatest fear, he admitted, was that his assessment was correct: that he was going crazy, and that the capable, self-reliant man he used to be was gone for good.

  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
